description: We are a team of 6 building a website for storytelling of NASA's abandoned equipments on Moon and Mars which contributed to the science and technology ,in a fun and interactive way so that it's interesting for the students to learn from it.
summary: HexaVoyagers is a single-page, responsive web application that tells the stories of abandoned and retired space missions through interactive, data-driven storytelling. We compiled mission data from NASA archives, Wikipedia, and other public sources, then structured it into narrative sections covering Opportunity, Cassini, Voyager 1, Philae and Rosetta, Curiosity, and InSight, plus a catalog of failed and cancelled missions grouped by category. The site is built with HTML, CSS, and JavaScript, with dynamically rendered content, a scored quiz module, a Star Catcher mini-game, a sources and credits section, and accessibility features. The project was developed through AI-assisted prompt engineering with Claude, followed by our own review and curation of the content. It turns raw mission data into an engaging learning experience that builds science literacy and preserves the legacy of humanity's silent explorers.
details:
What it does: HexaVoyagers is an interactive website that tells the stories of abandoned, retired, and lost space missions. Visitors scroll through narrative sections on Opportunity, Cassini, Voyager 1, Philae and Rosetta, Curiosity, and InSight, browse a catalog of failed and cancelled missions grouped by category, and test what they learned with a scored quiz and the Star Catcher mini-game.
Benefits and impact: Space missions are usually remembered for their launches, not their endings. We present mission data as emotional, human-centered stories to make space history engaging and accessible, build science literacy, and encourage curiosity about space exploration. The site is also designed with accessibility features and works on both phones and desktops.
Tools and technologies: HTML, CSS, and JavaScript, with dynamically rendered content, deployed on Vercel. Mission data came from NASA resources, Wikipedia, and other public sources, which are listed in the site's Sources and Credits section. We used Claude (a Super Intelligence tool) through prompting to help with coding, debugging, and research, and we reviewed and curated the results ourselves.
Creativity: Instead of presenting dry facts, we gave the machines a voice. Titles like "Left Behind but Not Forgotten" and the "quiet graveyard of human ambition" frame each mission's ending as part of its legacy.
Factors considered: Data accuracy, proper source attribution, readability, accessibility, and an engaging experience for all ages.
